teaching.causalExplanation: Here's the thirty-five degree launch. It sails over. Now the sideways launch, same speed. It hits the wall. So a wall lower than the cliff guarantees nothing. What matters is how high the ball is at one moment, the moment it reaches the wall's horizontal position. How far above the wall top it passes then is called the clearance. Finding it is our whole question. Let's set it up. Put the origin at the launch point, with up as positive, so a y is minus nine point eight metres per second squared. The sea is fifteen metres below the launch point, and the wall top is eight metres above the sea. Eighteen metres per second is the size of the launch velocity, not either component, so resolve it: u x is eighteen cos thirty-five, about fourteen point seven metres per second, and u y is eighteen sin thirty-five, about ten point three, upwards. Keep the unrounded values in your calculator. And the wall is twenty-five metres away horizontally. Which column can tell us when the ball reaches the wall? Not the vertical one, because the height there is exactly what we don't know. But we do know the horizontal distance, and horizontally the ball keeps a constant velocity. So s x equals u x t, which gives t equals twenty-five over fourteen point seven four, about one point six nine six seconds. Two columns, one clock, but this time the horizontal column sets the clock, and the time carries across.

scenes.teachingReason: Last time we found where a ball lands when it's launched from a cliff. Now there's something in the way. This ball leaves a cliff top fifteen metres above the sea, at eighteen metres per second, thirty-five degrees above the horizontal. Twenty-five metres out stands a wall, eight metres tall, measured from sea level. The wall is lower than the cliff, so surely it clears? And what if the ball were launched straight sideways at the same speed? Make a prediction.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the thirty-five degree launch. It sails over. Now the sideways launch, same speed. It hits the wall. So a wall lower than the cliff guarantees nothing. What matters is how high the ball is at one moment, the moment it reaches the wall's horizontal position. How far above the wall top it passes then is called the clearance. Finding it is our whole question.

scenes.teachingReason: Let's set it up. Put the origin at the launch point, with up as positive, so a y is minus nine point eight metres per second squared. The sea is fifteen metres below the launch point, and the wall top is eight metres above the sea. Eighteen metres per second is the size of the launch velocity, not either component, so resolve it: u x is eighteen cos thirty-five, about fourteen point seven metres per second, and u y is eighteen sin thirty-five, about ten point three, upwards. Keep the unrounded values in your calculator. And the wall is twenty-five metres away horizontally.

scenes.teachingReason: Now use that time in the vertical column. s y equals u y t plus a half a y t squared. The first term is how high the launch velocity alone would carry the ball by then, ten point three two times one point six nine six, about seventeen point five metres. The second term is how far gravity has pulled it back down in the same time, four point nine t squared, about fourteen point one metres. Subtract, and the ball is three point four two metres above the launch point when it reaches the wall. It's already past its peak and falling, but it's still above the cliff top.

scenes.teachingReason: Careful here. Three point four two metres is measured from the launch point, but the wall is measured from the sea. Heights only compare when they're measured from one datum, one level that every height is measured from. Take sea level. The launch point is fifteen metres up, so the ball is at fifteen plus three point four two, eighteen point four two metres above the sea. The wall top is at eight. So the clearance is eighteen point four two minus eight, ten point four two, about ten point four metres. Yes, it clears.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's a trap worth seeing. Suppose you round u y to ten point three two and the time to one point seven zero seconds, then round each term to three figures. Seventeen point five minus fourteen point two gives three point three. That's twelve centimetres too low, and the clearance comes out as ten point three instead of ten point four. Subtracting two big, nearly equal numbers magnifies any rounding in them. So keep the full values in your calculator, and round only the final answer.
